value.overview: The Rufous-browed Tyrannulet is a small, active tyrant flycatcher of humid mountain forests in Central and northern South America. It is recognized by its olive-green upperparts, pale underparts, and distinctive rufous or rusty eyebrow. The species often remains high in the forest canopy, where it makes short flights to capture insects from leaves and twigs. Its distribution is patchy, and it can be difficult to detect despite its lively calls and restless behavior.
value.classification: The Rufous-browed Tyrannulet belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Phylloscartes. It is divided into several geographically separated populations or subspecies across Central and South America.
value.identification: This small tyrannulet has olive-green upperparts, a yellowish to pale underside, and a strongly contrasting rusty-rufous eyebrow extending behind the eye. The wings show contrasting darker flight feathers and pale edging, while the bill is short and slender. It is usually seen moving quickly through foliage, often perched horizontally with the tail slightly raised. Its high, lively song and sharp calls can be more useful for detection than its unobtrusive appearance.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a disjunct range from Costa Rica and western Panama south through parts of Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, and northern Peru. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly on the Caribbean slope, from the Cordillera de Guanacaste eastward through the Cordillera Central, generally in humid montane evergreen forest at roughly 600–1,200 meters, with some populations or records reaching higher elevations. It uses mature forest, forest edges, and sometimes adjacent wooded habitats with dense foliage.
value.migrationStatus: The Rufous-browed Tyrannulet is considered a year-round resident rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, it remains in suitable humid mountain forests throughout the year, although local movements may occur in response to food availability or weather.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited. In Costa Rica, breeding is thought to occur mainly from March through May or June. The species is believed to nest in forest vegetation, but details about nest construction, clutch size, incubation, and care of young remain poorly documented. Its breeding season coincides with the beginning and middle of Costa Rica’s wetter period, when insect food is generally abundant in montane forests.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet is thought to consist mainly of insects and other small arthropods, with small fruits possibly taken occasionally. It forages actively in the canopy and sometimes at lower levels, making short sallies to hover-glean prey from leaves and twigs. Individuals may forage alone, in pairs, or in small family groups, and they often join mixed-species feeding flocks.
value.behavior: The Rufous-browed Tyrannulet is energetic and quick-moving. It frequently shifts between exposed perches and leafy branches, raising or cocking its tail and making brief flights to inspect nearby foliage. It regularly participates in mixed-species flocks, which may help it locate food or detect predators. The species is more often heard than seen in dense forest, giving high, sharp, lively calls and a rapidly delivered song.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is believed to be decreasing, although the rate of decline is not well quantified.
conservation.threats: The principal potential threat is loss and fragmentation of humid montane forest, especially through agricultural expansion, logging, and other changes to forest structure. Its patchy distribution and dependence on mature, humid woodland may make local populations vulnerable when suitable habitat is isolated.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore humid montane forest, maintain connected forest corridors, and reduce clearing and degradation along mountain slopes. In Costa Rica, supporting protected areas and responsible management of forested watersheds can help preserve the species’ habitat. Careful bird monitoring is also valuable because the species is local and inconspicuous, and its population status is not well known.
